15. It will be evident from the above narration that the plaintiffs were non-suited only on the ground that Himangshu and Arunangshu, their co-sharers in the suit land, were not made parties to the suit. Leave was granted to consider whether the High Court Division was right in holding in the circumstances of the case that the suit was bad for defect of party and was liable to be dismissed altogether on that ground. 

 17. As regard B schedule land it appears that there is some confusion in the findings of the learned Subordinate Judge with regard to the non-inctusion of Himangshu and Arunangshu in the suit and its effect thereon. Plaintiff no.2 deposing as P.W.1 in 1976 admitted that Himangshu and Arunangshu are staying in India but it is nobody's case that they were enemy within the meaning of rule 161 of the Defence of Pakistan Rules 1965 and their shares in B schedule land became enemy property within the meaning of rule 169(4) of the said Rules. The learned Subordinate Judge himself noticed that the defendants have not specifically stated in their written statement as to who were the persons who having left for India became Indian Nationals and their shares became enemy property. In one place of the Judgment the learned Subordinate Judge has expressed the view that since amicable partition was not proved and there being no evidence that Himangshu and Arunangshu have left their shares, non-inclusion of them in the suit, who were admittedly co-sharers, rendered the suit bad for defect of parties. It appears however, from his ultimate finding that he has treated the shares of Himangshu and Arunangshu as enemy property (without any basis) as they are living in India and held that without a partition of the suit property in respect of their sheres the defendants cannot take over possession of the suit land and lease out the same. If Himangshu and Arunangshus share is treated as enemy share then there is no question of defect of parties because the enemy will he taken to be represented by the Assistant Custodian, Enemy Property (Land and Building) respondent no. 1. The view taken by the learned Subordinate Judge that the defendants cannot take over possession without a partition of the suit land in respect of the shares of Himangshu and Arunangshu (if they are enemy) is fully in accord with the law laid down in the case of Benoy Bhushan Vs. S.D.O. Brahmanharia, 30 DLR(SC)(1978) 139, We do not, therefore, see how the plaintiffs could be refused the relief of injunction at least even in respect of B schedule land after having made the finding as aforesaid. 

 20. Mr. S.S. Haider, learned Advocate for the appellants, has submitted that the plaintiffs being admittedly co-sharers in possession of the entire land and the suit being for the benefit of all the co-sharers and there being no possibility of any decree which is likely to be prejudicial to the interest of other co-sharers only, the suit cannot fail on the ground of alleged defect of party. Mr. Haider has referred to Order I Rule of 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure and argued that in any case the suit could not be defeated because nonjoinder of Himangshu and Arunangstu as the Court could decide the matter in controversy so far as regards the rights and interests of the parties actually before it. He drew our attention to Abdul Rahman Vs. Abdul Jabbar, 13 D.L.R. 576 in which a Division Bench held that a suit can proceed when the rights of an absent party are not affected by the decision. 

 29. Thus the main question is, whether the suit has been rightly dismissed for non impleading necessary parties which is a pre requisite in law for proper constitution of the suit. 

 "That the petition of the principal defdt. No.3 submitted in the E.P.Case No.10/74-75 on which the principal defdt. No.2 passed an order on 27.8.74 specifically speaks that the suit properties belong to the plff. Nos.1,4 and others. So the plff. have come up with this suit and their co-sharers have been made proforma defdts. If any of the proforma defdt. contests the suit he may be treated as a principal defdt." Admittedly these two Sons of Harimohan Paul were not made parties in the suit and hence the pertinent question for consideration in this appeal is, whether for non inclusion of these two co-sharers as parties any incurable defect has arisen for which the suit must fail. 

 35. We must bear in mind the distinction between a "necessary" and "proper" party as contemplated under Order 1, Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure. A necessary party is one whose presence on the record is enjoined by law or in whose absence no effective decision can at all be given and without that person suit cannot be properly constituted and liable to be dismissed. A "proper" party, on the other hand, is one whose presence is not essential in the constitution of the suit but whose presence is desirable in order to properly or completely adjudicate on the matter involved, if omission to implead necessary party is not corrected by the person bringing the suit, the suit is liable to be dismissed. A reference to Order 1, Rule 9 of the Code provides that no suit shall fail for non-joinder of parties. But this rule cannot be applied in a case where the proper constitution of the suit requires a necessary party to be on record. 

 Hence, I am to see whether the left out co sharers are necessary parties in this suit for declaration and permanent injunction. As per the averments of the plaint all the co-sharers including the left out co-sharers have subsisting interest in the property. If for any reason the plaintiffs could not implead Himangshu and Arunangshu in the category of plaintiffs. I cannot understand why the plaintiffs could not implead these co-sharers as defendants when the objection was raised at the earliest point of time by the contesting defendants. In this suit it is not possible to split up the joint interest of the parties in the land. It is further found that the plaintiffs are not suing in their personal capacity but suing as co-sharers in possession of the suit land. It is quite clear that the plaintiffs filed the suit on specific averments of joint interest in an unpartitioned land and having sued in that capacity all must be brought on record. It cannot be said that the left out co-sharers are not jointly interested in the immovable property and that being the position they must be brought on record as they have direct interest in the suit property. In a suit for declaration and permanent injunction if the plaintiffs get a decree then the same conclusively binds all the parties and in that event it is undisputed that the suit ought to have been heard in presence of all the co-sharers for an effective decree within the frame of the suit. The main averments is that, all the co-sharers are interested in all the lands but the plaintiffs are in possession as co-owners and in that view a cosharer in possession is certainly entitled under the law to maintain a suit for declaration and permanent injunction to protect his proprietary right in it but all joint owners must be on record for proper constitution of the suit as they are jointly interested in the subject matter of the suit. Thus, I find that the plaintiffs suit is in fact defective for want of necessary parties and it cannot proceed. This being a case of declaration of title and permanent injunction the plaintiff is oblige to make out a case of good title for all the co-sharers and this issue of title could not be decided leaving these two admitted co-sharers. Section 53 of the Specific Relief Act says that a decree for permanent injunction can only be granted upon the merits of the suit. The plaintiffs story of amicable partition of "B' schedule properties and acquisition of absolute ownership by the plaintiffs was not accepted by the courts below. Further, the division of 'A' schedule properties by metes and bounds was also not accepted by the courts below. Hence, right, title and interest cannot be finally concluded without the necessary parties. In a suit for declaration and perpetual injunction the plaintiff must first establish his legal right. After the plaintiff succeeds in establishing his legal right and its violation he is granted a permanent injunction. Permanent injunction can be granted by the decree made at the hearing and upon the merits of a suit which concludes a right for ever. Thus, unless the rights of all persons who have joint right, title and interest are brought on record, no violation of right of all persons can be determined. Thus it is very simple that all joint owners must be on record. Where there is a joint right it may be necessary for all persons jointly interested to be joined as parties, and if they are not joined the suit will be bad for misjoinder. The immovable property being jointly owned each co-owner is in theory Interested in every portion of the suit land and each has a right, irrespective of the quantity of his share. Due to the conflicting averments and adverse claim which was not accepted by the courts blow, the co-owners ought to have been made parties. In paragraph 16 of the plaint it has been stated that all the co-sharers have been made proforma defendants. This factual assertion is also not correct as admittedly two of the co-sharers are left out. Further, there is averments that if any of the proforma defendant contests the suit he may be treated as a principal defendant. Hence it is palpable to say that the plaintiffs have got no consent to file the suit on behalf of these left out co sharers and that their interest is also adverse to be plaintiffs interest. From the very beginning of the suit the objection as to non-joinder of necessary parties was raised specifically in the written statement, even then the plaintiff did not care to implead these two admitted co-sharers namely. Himangshu and Arunangshu as parties. This is one of the circumstances also which lends support to the fact that the plaintiffs are claiming as if they are only heirs of Harimohan Paul. 

 In the case of Allam Gangadhara Rao V. Gollapalli Gangarao, AIR 1968 Andhpra 291 it has been held that even in the case of persons jointly entitled to any relief, the language of R. I of O.1 C.P.C. says that all such persons may be joined in one suit, either as plaintiffs or defendants. The reason is that such persons together represent a single and indivisible right which cannot be adjudicated upon and no effective decree can be passed by the Court in absence of such persons. In Aswini Kumar V. Kshitish Chandra, AIR 1971 Cal 252, which was a case for declaration of title and recovery of possession, it was held that the suit becomes incompetent if some of the co-owners are not impleaded as parties. In the case of Kanakaranthanamaly Vs. Loganath Mudaliar, AIR 1965 SC 271, a dispute arose relating to the property purchased by the wife with money gifted by the husband in a suit by daughter to recover property from beneficiary under will of father. The brothers were not impleaded as parties. It was held that the suit was incompetent for non-joinder of necessary parties. In the case of Kanakarathanammal Vs. VS. Loganatha Mudaliar and another reported in A.I.R. 1965 SC-271, it has been observed as follows:- 

 "It is true that under O. 1, R. 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure no suit shall be defeated by reason of the misjoinder or non-joinder of the parties, but there can be no doubt that if the parties who are not joined are not only proper but also necessary parties to it, the infirmity in the suit is bound to be fatal. Even in such cases; the Court can under O. 1, R. 10, sub-rule 2 direct the necessary parties to be joined, but all this can and should be done at the stage of trial and that too without prejudice to the said parties plea of limitation.
